questions.question: Explain rural–urban migration as a balance of push and pull factors, including the role of perception and the selectivity of who moves.
questions.expected_answer: Push factors are conditions at home that drive people out: rural unemployment as farms mechanise and plots shrink, weak schools, distant clinics, poor roads and unreliable services, drought and land degradation, and the absence of opportunity for the young. Pull factors are the city's attractions, real or believed: jobs and higher wages, education, hospitals, reliable services, and relatives who moved earlier and offer a first bed. Migration happens when the combined shove and tug outweigh the comfort of staying. Migrants often move on the perception of opportunity — the city does not always deliver, and many arrive to unemployment and informal housing. The movement is selective: mainly young, economically active adults, historically men first through the migrant labour system, which is why the settlements left behind become unbalanced.

questions.question: Describe the consequences of rural depopulation for the people who remain and for the place itself, and give a balanced evaluation.
questions.expected_answer: For the people: a hollowed-out age–sex structure — children, the elderly and mostly women remain while the working-age middle is missing; dependence on social grants and remittances; a rising dependency ratio; and a brain drain as the skilled and ambitious leave first. For the place: fields fall out of cultivation while nearby grazing is overused, buildings decay, schools and shops close, and the consumer and tax base evaporates — the closed shopfronts of some Free State platteland towns show the end state. The balance: remittances flow back and build houses, pressure on communal land eases, and some migrants return with skills and savings — heavy costs with modest compensations.

questions.question: Distinguish the three legs of land reform — tenure, redistribution and restitution — and explain how successful land reform counters depopulation.
questions.expected_answer: Tenure reform strengthens the rights of people already on the land — farm dwellers, labour tenants and communal residents — protecting them from arbitrary eviction without moving anyone. Redistribution changes ownership going forward, assisting black South Africans to acquire farmland for equity and livelihoods, historically through willing-buyer, willing-seller purchases. Restitution looks backward: people dispossessed of specific land after 19 June 1913 by racially discriminatory laws can claim that land back or receive compensation, through the restitution commission and Land Claims Court. In short: strengthen, share, return. Done well, land reform is itself an anti-depopulation strategy, because secure rights on productive land give rural families a livelihood at home — the very thing migration promises — without leaving.
